previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with end-stage renal disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and antiphospholipid syndrome was admitted for failure to thrive and significant weight loss following a recent hospitalization for post-ERCP pancreatitis. She reported poor oral intake, early satiety, nausea, and difficulty maintaining nutrition at home. During admission, her oral intake improved with dietary modifications, including a switch to clear Nepro supplements, and calorie counts confirmed adequate intake. Her weight stabilized at 42 kg. A subtherapeutic INR of 1.1 was identified, prompting initiation of a heparin drip to bridge anticoagulation until warfarin achieved a therapeutic INR of 1.6. Orthostatic hypotension led to a temporary hold and subsequent dose reduction of labetalol. She remained on home medications including lamotrigine, omeprazole, and trazodone, with no psychiatric medication changes. Hemodialysis was continued throughout the stay. Discharge planning included warfarin dose adjustment, INR monitoring at dialysis, daily weight checks, and coordination with elder services for grocery assistance. She was discharged home in stable condition with improved nutrition and therapeutic anticoagulation.

History of Present Illness:
Ms. ___ is a ___ female with a history of 
___ deficiency, chronic dizziness, ESRD s/p failed renal 
transplant on HD, who presents today complaining of dizziness, 
weakness. 

At 8 am on day of presentation she was making breakfast and 
noted acute onset of general weakness, dizziness, poor balance, 
and mild confusion.  She did not fall, but felt as though she 
was losing her balance in all directions and had to sit down. 
She had trouble with hand grip, particularly in her right hand.  
When she went to dial the phone, she was unable to correctly 
input the number. At the time she did not have a headache.  She 
had double vision, initially in all directions and forward gaze. 
It has since improved and now she has double vision with only 
left lateral gaze. Her ""dizziness"" was feeling off balance and 
""feeling that I was moving and that the room was moving, but not 
spinning."" This sensation was made worse by moving her head or 
having to move her body (on/off stretchers, etc). The majority 
of her symptoms did not improve until she was in the ED; she 
feels that they improved/resolved shortly after being given the 
calcium, insulin, and glucose for her high potassium.  

She developed a headache in the afternoon, after coming to the 
ED.  She's had ongoing nausea, no vomiting. She had shortness of 
breath that has improved. She has chronic constipation no 
change. No diarrhea, no fevers, chills. She endorses getting 
night sweats on dialysis nights, no change in last several 
weeks. She does not make any urine. No recent URI symptoms. No 
cough. No chest pain. She has stable shortness of breath 
(?desaturations) intermittently with exertion (walking 50 feet, 
going up stairs), which is at baseline. Despite her 
bleeding/clotting disorders, she has not experienced any recent 
bleeding, melena, BRBPR, or any other blood loss.  She 
frequently has abdominal pain due to a retained stone in her 
biliary duct, for which she uses PO dilaudid at home. This pain 
is stable. No rashes.  

She denies medication noncompliance.

In the ED her inital vitals were: 97.1 60 133/80 18 100% ra. 
Labs were significant for K of 7.1.   Her HR was bradycardic to 
low of 35, asymptomatic, and otherwise in 50-60's. She was given 
10 units regular insulin, dextrose 50% 25gm, and calcium 
gluconate 1g and evluated by the neurology service for a code 
stroke. They believe the chance of stroke less likely given 
constellation of symptoms, with migraine equivalent more likely. 


She was then transferred for HD, after which she was taken to 
the floor.  Vitals upon transfer: 45 162/68 20 100%.

On the floor, she complains of extreme hunger, headache, 
irritability, but states her weakness, dizziness, and other 
symptoms have greatly improved/resovled.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ female with multiple medical 
coborbidities, including a history SLE, ___ deficiency 
c/b bleeding and DVTs, ESRD s/p failed renal transplant on HD, 
who was diagnosed with uremia, electrolyte abnormalities 
(hyperkalemia), and atypical migraines causing weakness, 
confusion, and disequilibrium.

# Hyperkalemia - Admit K 7.1 with peaked T's on EKG. Resolved 
after dialysis. She was given calcium, insulin, and glucose in 
the ED.

# Dizziness, weakness, neurologic symptoms - Initially thought 
to be a combination of uremia (BUN 106), hyperkalemia (7.1), and 
atypical migraines given the resolution over several hours at 
HD. Speaking with her outpatient nephrologist, Dr. ___ 
seems less likely to be due to electrolyte abnormalities given 
that she frequently has uremia and hyperkalemia.  She did not 
have clinical signs of seizure, and reported that her previous 
seizures had been generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Since her 
symptoms had almost resolved by the time she arrived to the 
floor, an EEG was deferred.  She was evaluated by neurology 
stroke service in the ED, who found low suspicion for stroke and 
no further imaging after the non-con head CT was pursued. No 
infectious signs or symptoms. At discharge, felt to be most 
likely atypical migraines, as she has had them in the past and 
had a post-drome (angry, tired, headache, etc) that resolved 
after sleeping. She was walking laps, cheery and chatty without 
neurologic symptoms at discahrge.

# Bradycardia - Low HR to 35 in the ED, which was likely related 
to electrolyte abnormalities, in particular hyperkalemia.  
Watched on tele overnight, with no bradycardia or events.  Tele 
was discontinued in the AM as she develops contact dermatitis to 
adhesive. 

# APLS/hyperfibrinolytic syndrome/Anticoagulation - On warfarin 
for ALPS, DVTs with goal INR 1.5-2.5 and managed by her 
nephrologist Dr. ___ was subtherapeutic at 1.3. Bridging 
was discussed with her outpatient provider and deferred, however 
her weekly regimen was increased by 1mg by increasing her 
alternating schedule to 4mg 4x/week and 3mg 3x/week. 

# Thrombocytopenia - She has had thrombocytopenia in the past 
(last year) however more recent values have been WNL. No source 
of bleeding or clotting clinically identified, so felt unlikely 
to be consumptive. Etiology unclear. Plan to trend as 
outpatient.

# OSA - She refused CPAP while inpatient. 
# Skin reaction to tele leads - Topical clobetisol was 
continued. 
# Seizure disorder: continued home lamotrigine. This 
antiepileptic could be contributing to nystagmus.
# ESRD on HD: Continued outpatient HD schedule. 
# CODE: Full code, confirmed with patient.
# CONTACT: Sister, ___, is HCP. ___

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure caring for you at ___. You were admitted 
with weakness, feeling off balance, and confusion. Our neurology 
stroke team evaluated you and believe that your symptoms are 
unlike to be due to a stroke, but could be due to atypical 
migraines.  Another large contributing factor was your 
electrolyte imbalances.  You had a blood urea nitrogen that was 
greater than 100, which can cause confusion and weakness, and 
you had a high potassium level as well. Your symptoms improved 
after these values were treated and you were dialyzed. We are 
discharging you home to follow up with your primary care 
physician and nephrologist. Please continue to take your 
medications and adhere to a renal diet (especially low 
potassium).

We also changed your warfarin dosing so that you take 1 
additional milligram a week, as you were below your target. 
Please see medication list for details.

Sincerely,
Your ___ medicine team
